summary: Defines optional Diameter attributes for networks that use Explicit Congestion Notification or Diameter traffic filters. They improve traffic identification and ECN support and reduce the effort of filter administration, extending the Filter-Rule AVP from RFC 5777.

eli5.summary: These are extra labels that let a network describe traffic more exactly and handle traffic jams more gracefully.

questions: how does diameter support traffic filters
subtitle: Four new Diameter attributes for matching ECN-marked traffic, reacting to congestion and counting flows and packets.

tldr.problem: The Diameter Filter-Rule from RFC 5777 cannot match packets by their ECN marking, cannot specify an action when the matched flows are congested, and cannot report how many flows or packets a filter covers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four optional AVPs: ECN-IP-Codepoint (628), Congestion-Treatment (629), Flow-Count (630) and Packet-Count (631), which plug into the RFC 5777 structures.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can classify ECN traffic, set an alternate treatment under congestion and get flow and packet counts in accounting. The attributes are forward and backwards compatible with RFC 5777.

today: RFC 7660 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It extends the Filter-Rule machinery of RFC 5777 and its attributes are described as forward and backwards compatible with it.

sections.title: The Gap in Diameter Filters
sections.content:
Diameter is the base protocol in RFC 6733, and RFC 5777 defines the Filter-Rule AVP, which can carry classification, conditions and actions. RFC 7660 points out three gaps. Filter-Rule cannot identify packets that use Explicit Congestion Notification (RFC 3168), gives no specific action when the described flows are congested, and can describe many flows without saying how many there are. Flow counts and related data such as packets are not captured by accounting applications, so administrators lack information about how effective a filter is.

The document adds four optional AVPs to fill these gaps. Two relate to ECN: one matches ECN-marked traffic and the other defines alternate treatment under congestion. Two, Flow-Count and Packet-Count, convey information about the group of flows a filter describes. All are Diameter AVPs written in the modified ABNF of RFC 6733.
sections.eli5: The old rules could not tell warning-flagged cars apart, did not say what to do in a jam, and could not count cars. These new labels fix all three.

sections.title: ECN-IP-Codepoint and Congestion-Treatment
sections.content:
The ECN-IP-Codepoint AVP (code 628, type Enumerated) names the ECN codepoint to match in the IP header. When used for classification in a Filter-Rule it MUST be part of the Classifier grouped AVP from RFC 5777.

The Congestion-Treatment AVP (code 629, type Grouped) says how to treat IP 5-tuple flows when congestion is detected. Detection can be based on packets with the Congestion Experienced (CE) codepoint set, or on any other administratively defined criteria. It applies to all packets of all 5-tuples captured by the Filter-Rule. If the AVP is absent, the treatment of congested traffic is left to the discretion of the node doing quality-of-service treatment.

It contains a required Treatment-Action, an optional QoS-Profile-Template and optional QoS-Parameters, all defined in RFC 5777. Because it is an action, it MUST be an attribute of the Filter-Rule grouped AVP.
sections.eli5: One label says which warning flag a car has. The other says what to do with those cars when the road gets jammed. If nobody says, the traffic cop decides.

sections.title: Flow-Count and Packet-Count
sections.content:
Flow-Count (code 630) and Packet-Count (code 631) are both of type Unsigned64. They give the number of protocol-specific flows or packets, where the protocol is determined by the filter, for example an IPFilterRule or a Filter-Id.

They describe the group of flows a Filter-Rule, IPFilterRule or other Diameter traffic filter covers. Congestion-management functions can use them to learn how many flows are congested, and administrators can use them to judge the impact of a filter definition.
sections.eli5: One counter says how many separate trips happened and the other says how many cars drove by, for whatever group of traffic a rule covers.

sections.title: Examples and Credit Control Use
sections.content:
In the Classifier example, ECN-IP-Codepoint is added as an optional member of the RFC 5777 Classifier AVP (code 511). Setting it to CE captures the CE flags in the flow. A second Classifier with the value ECT, combined with Flow-Count, reports the number of ECT-capable flows.

In Diameter Credit Control, a node can use Congestion-Treatment to trigger actions when congestion occurs, similar to the Excess-Treatment action. If either has occurred, Diameter clients may autonomously send Credit-Control Requests during the service session as interim events. Flow-Count and Packet-Count can ride in the CCR, giving the credit control server a better view of the congested traffic for decisions and charging.

The RFC adds that sending these AVPs under any condition permits rudimentary traffic profiling: low byte counts per packet indicate web traffic, and high byte counts per packet with few flows may indicate video. It states this reporting relieves Deep Packet Inspection load as traffic becomes more encrypted. Where a service limits the number of flows rather than bytes, Flow-Count may be used in place of Service-Units.
sections.eli5: A shop that sells by the trip rather than by the pound can count trips. And just by seeing a few big trucks or lots of little cars, you can guess what kind of traffic it is without opening any boxes.

sections.title: AVP Codes
sections.content: IANA allocated the four codes in the AVP namespace registry defined in Section 11.1.1 of RFC 6733. They are ECN-IP-Codepoint 628 (Enumerated), Congestion-Treatment 629 (Grouped), Flow-Count 630 (Unsigned64) and Packet-Count 631 (Unsigned64).
sections.eli5: Each new label gets its own official number so everyone uses the same one.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC says the new filter parameter and the Congestion-Treatment AVP are extensions of RFC 5777 that reuse its attributes, so they do not raise new security concerns. Use of the AVPs MUST take into account the security issues and requirements of the Diameter base protocol.

Flow-Count and Packet-Count provide more information that can be privacy sensitive, in proportion to the traffic captured by filters and reports. Narrow filtering gives the highest sensitivity but is too resource intensive for large networks. If an administrator can apply congestion actions without reporting them to a Diameter application, they should use Congestion-Treatment, which also reduces Diameter traffic during congestion.
sections.eli5: Counting more things tells people a little more about what is going on, so be careful who sees the counts.
